cognate: *suHnú- ~ υἱός; *h₁nómn̥ ~ nā́man ~ ὄνομα; *dʰeh₁- ~ dadhé ~ ἔθηκε; *ḱlew- in śrávase ~ κλεεννόν
drift_or_renewal: κλεεννόν (in the passage's preceding context line, mapped 'unmapped' in the slab) is a *ḱlew- derivative. Fame is expressed by the dative of purpose śrávase in Vedic but by a predicative adjective κλεεννόν (a *ḱléwes-no- derivative) in Greek; Vedic middle 'took on a name for himself' vs Greek active 'made (his father's) name famous'; the RV parallels with the father's name use putrá- for 'son'
shared_syntax: subject 'son' + verb *dʰeh₁- + object *h₁nómn̥, with a *ḱlew- word stating the result (name set for fame / name set famous)
context: both are martial: in RV 1.103.4 Indra the club-bearer, setting out to kill the Dasyus, 'the son took on a name for fame'; in the epigram the spear-bearing son, fallen in a Thracian ambush, 'made his father Diphilos' name famous'. Each is about a warrior winning a glorious name by fighting. The plain naming phrase *h₁nómn̥ dʰeh₁- (nā́ma dhā-, ὄνομα θέσθαι) is a well-known inherited collocation. Here it is joined by the same subject (*suHnú-) and the same fame-root. Elsewhere in the RV the fame word recurs with nā́ma dhā- (10.28.12, 6.1.4), and so does the son setting the father's name (1.155.3, 9.75.2). So the combination is a stable Vedic pattern, not a one-off.
phrase: *suHnús h₁nómn̥ dʰeh₁- (ḱléwos): 'the son sets a name for fame'

cognate: *még̑h₂ ~ máhi ~ μέγα (here the superlative μέγιστον); *ḱléwos ~ śrávas ~ κλέος
drift_or_renewal: Pindar uses the superlative μέγιστον for the positive μέγα. The verb differs: Ved. ā́ dade 'took' (and elsewhere dhā-, rā-), Gk αὔξων 'increasing'. Ved. vardh- with śrávas (RV 8.15.8) is the semantic counterpart, not a cognate.
shared_syntax: neuter adjective + neuter noun in the same order (adjective first), the object of a verb of getting or increasing
context: in both, great fame is a prize that is won and passed on. In RV 9.61.10 Soma's birth 'took (ā́ dade) mighty protection and great fame'. In Pindar I. 7.29 the fallen warrior 'increased the greatest fame for the race of citizens'. In both corpora the phrase is formulaic: 24 RV units with máhi + śrávas, 13 Homeric lines with μέγα/μεῖζον/μέγιστον κλέος. The neuter 'great fame' equation is a standard item of Indo-European poetic phraseology.

cognate: *n̥-dʰgʷʰi-tó- ~ ákṣita- ~ ἄφθιτος; *gʷeyh₃- in jīvati / jīvātu- ~ βίοτος / ζῆν
drift_or_renewal: in AVŚ 18.4.s63 the DCS text splits the privative (a kṣitām), so the slab maps only kṣi; the word is akṣitā- = akṣita. The 'life' word differs in formation (Ved. verb jīvati and noun jīvātu-; Gk noun βίοτος, verb ζῆν), with the root kept. Ved. akṣita is applied to the life-giving food or cow on which one lives (upa jīv-), Gk to the life itself; both nouns mean 'life' as well as 'livelihood, sustenance'.
shared_syntax: *n̥dʰgʷʰitó- qualifying the life one lives: epithet + noun (jīvātum akṣitām ~ βίοτον ἄφθιτον), or the verb 'live' with an imperishable object or predicate (akṣitām upa jīvati, pitṝṇāṃ loke 'kṣitam ~ ζῆν ἄφθιτον)
context: in both the setting is life after death. AVŚ 18.4: the dead man 'lives on the imperishable (cow) in Yama's realm' and has an imperishable spring (utsam akṣitam); AVŚ 3.29.8 has the giver living on the imperishable in the world of the Fathers. Pindar O. 2.29: Ino, after death, is given 'imperishable life' among Nereus' daughters; Euripides Or. 1635: the deified Helen must 'live imperishable'. AVŚ 7.17.3 jīvātum akṣitām is the exact noun + epithet shape of βίοτον ἄφθιτον. Both traditions tie the inherited 'imperishable' adjective to the life of someone translated beyond death. This is more specific than the general ákṣita/ἄφθιτος equation (śrávas ákṣitam ~ κλέος ἄφθιτον), but 'imperishable life' is semantically natural and could have been formed independently.

note: All 155 AV-pivot bundles read; most partners are Greek/Latin prose with no shared wording. Three claims: máhi śrávas ~ μέγα κλέος (high); son + name + *dʰeh₁- + fame (medium); imperishable life after death (low). Rejected as generic/chance: ship+oar (B-84cf5/B-ade83), wiping the hand (B-cbb1d), widow and husband (B-d0f74), day/night merisms.
